zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical cross-checks used the supplied Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, licensed CC BY 4.0 (release: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). The scan-grounded readings and English review notes are this review's own work, not a replacement NINJAL transcription.

runs.text: Dizendo varias eſcuſas, ou outras couſas.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's Nanino cano example: giving various excuses or saying other things. The preceding catchword Dizendo correctly anticipates this row and is not an additional word in the continuous text.

runs.text: Adu. Palaura com que ſe louua,

lines.note: Naniſama is labeled an adverbial expression used to praise something. The entry's further intensifying sense continues below; it is not being glossed as the modern question about someone's identity.
Adds the sense of emphasizing or extolling something and begins a Japanese example. The nasal sign in algũa belongs over u, and the example continues on the next physical row.
Completes Naniſama xeiuo ireôzu, promising to apply great diligence or effort. The scan supplies the l in diligencia rather than OCR ditigencia; the Japanese future spelling ireôzu is preserved.

runs.text: ou por todas as vias trabalharei.

lines.note: Gives the alternative translation 'I shall work by every means'. It concludes the emphatic Naniſama example rather than introducing another headword.
Nanitaru can refer to something or nothing, depending on the accompanying verb. The source explicitly conditions the interpretation rather than treating the two glosses as unrelated meanings.

runs.text: ao verbo que ſe ajunta. Vt,

lines.note: Completes the explanation about the accompanying verb and begins Nanitaru cotomo. The physical co- is retained because the remainder of the Japanese expression occurs below.
Completes the negative example Nanitaru cotomo gozaranu, 'there is nothing'. Item then introduces the interrogative use on the next row; ha is retained without adding an accent here.
Gives the interrogative 'what thing?' and asks Nanitaru cotoga arǒca. The caron in arǒca is visible; the Portuguese translation follows rather than forming part of the Japanese sentence.
Translates the preceding question as 'what will there be?' A visible descending accent on the final a supports auerà, restoring the mark omitted by OCR without changing the historical u spelling.

runs.text: Adu. Como, ou de que maneira?

lines.note: Nanito asks 'how, or in what manner?' The adverbial label belongs to the Portuguese explanation, and both printed questions remain on this one row.

runs.text: De todas as maneiras, ou por to-

lines.note: Nanitomo is explained as 'in every way' or 'by every means'. To- is the beginning of Portuguese todas across the line break, not part of the Japanese headword.
Completes todas as vias and begins an example of being troubled in every respect. Meiuacuni retains the source's attached particle and historical spelling.

Completes the example and translates it as being distressed in every way. The tightly joined Portodas and the absence of a clear terminal stop are preserved instead of being regularized to modern prose.
Nanitomo xite asks by what means something can be done. Na- begins the repeated expression in its example on the following row, so the physical hyphen is retained.

Completes the question 'how shall I escape this hardship?' The source's nanguiuo refers to the difficulty, and nogareôzu carries the future or deliberative force reflected in the following translation.

runs.text: De que maneira eſcaparei deſte trabalho?

lines.note: Gives the Portuguese question 'how shall I escape this hardship?' Trabalho here corresponds to nangui, difficulty or trouble, not merely employment.
Nanitote asks why or how. The supplied division Por que is retained because the narrow printed spacing does not establish a different word division conclusively.
Nanito xitacotoni is an adverbial question about the cause or reason. The clear terminal question mark replaces the OCR full stop, while the printed Porque remains joined.
Refers the reader to Nanino cano for the 'this and that' or various-pretexts expression. The headword's printed division differs from the preceding page's example and is not harmonized.

runs.text: P. i, Axi. Caninhas, ou caniços

lines.note: Naniuaguſa is equated with Axi, reeds, and glossed as small canes or reeds. The visibly sloping P and Axi are retained in italic type; Axi is a synonym after i, not a Japanese word embedded in a Portuguese sentence.

Completes the reed definition by specifying those found in lagoons or pools. The historical alagoas is retained. The small accent above the a in hà is unevenly inked; the supplied grave is retained provisionally, not replaced by a modern accent.
Nanixini is printed with an interrogative mark and glossed 'why? or how?' Both the Japanese question mark and the two Portuguese questions remain visible in the transcription.

runs.text: O fazer com difficuldade, ou repug-

lines.note: This Nanjǔ concerns doing something with difficulty or reluctance. The second pass confirms two f ascenders in difficuldade, restoring the printed doubled consonant. The caron over u is visible, and repug- continues the Portuguese noun across the physical break.
Completes 'doing something with reluctance' and begins Nanjǔni voyobu. The example's verb is divided voyo-bu by the printed line ending; no expanded translation is inserted into the text.

runs.text: ¶ Item, ter dò, ou difficuldade co-

lines.note: Completes voyobu and introduces reluctance or difficulty, with giving-related examples below. Second-pass enlargement confirms the two f ascenders in difficuldade. The damaged interior does not establish a separate word, so the OCR split difficulda de is joined while retaining its printed doubled consonant.

runs.text: mo de dar, ou empreſtar, ou reſtituir. Vt,

lines.note: Specifies giving, lending, or returning something as occasions for reluctance. The scan supports reſtituir rather than reſtiluir and the example marker Vt rather than OCR Et.

Gives Nanjǔſuru and begins an injunction against reluctance toward virtuous conduct. Ienguiǒni is kept in the printed historical form; the injunction's negative ending and Portuguese translation follow.
Completes the prohibition coto nacare, 'do not be reluctant'. The Portuguese translation continues with the object of repugnancia on the next row rather than ending after the accented preposition.
Completes 'do not have an aversion to virtue'. This single-word row closes the ethical example under Nanjǔ and is preserved as a separate physical line.
A separate Nanjǔ is explained as Minamino foxi and glossed as the antarctic pole. The source's anthartico spelling is preserved; this is not the preceding word for reluctance.
Adds 'or star of the south' as the alternative gloss. This records the dictionary's wording without supplying a modern astronomical identification.

runs.text: Nanmen. Minami vomote. i, Minami mu-

lines.note: Nanmen denotes a southern aspect or south-facing position. The Japanese explanations Minami vomote and Minami muqi are separate from the Portuguese sentence, with mu- physically continued below.

runs.text: O eſtar peraa parte do Sul, como cus-

lines.note: Completes muqi and begins the explanation of facing south. The close peraa is retained as supplied, and cus- belongs to Portuguese custumão across the row break.

runs.text: tumão eſtar os Reys de Iapão, & da China.

lines.note: Completes custumão and reports the source's account of the customary orientation of rulers in Japan and China. The historical Reys and Iapão are preserved rather than normalized.

Begins the maxim about the ruler facing south and the retainer facing north. Nanmenxi restores the scan's letter count rather than OCR nanmnenxi; the unusual printed xinna is retained, not silently changed to expected xinua.

runs.text: O Reyeſta virado pera a parte do Sul,

lines.note: Completes focumenſu and translates the ruler's southward orientation. The tight Reyeſta join is retained; the Portuguese contrast with the retainers continues below.

runs.text: & os criados defronte delle pera a parte do

lines.note: Continues with the retainers standing opposite the ruler and facing the other direction. Delle refers back to the ruler, and the final direction is supplied on the next row.
Completes 'toward the north', closing the contrast between ruler and retainers. This short physical continuation is not a separate dictionary entry.
This Nanmon is a southern gate, explained as Minamino cado. The Portuguese gloss identifies an outer or street gate, with the directional phrase continued below.
Completes the gate's orientation 'toward the south'. It belongs to the directional Nanmon, not the following homophonous entry for a difficult question.
A second Nanmon means a difficult question. The scan's st-type ligature supports Queſtão rather than OCR Queſião, and the terminal S is upright rather than part of the italic Portuguese gloss.
Nannho pairs man and woman, with Votoco and vonna as the Japanese equivalents. The Portuguese likewise gives 'man and woman'; the source's molher spelling is retained.
Nanno asks 'what, or which?' Its example begins a question about the reason or circumstances, retaining xiſaide as printed rather than changing the historical romanization.
Completes Nanno xiſaide gozaruzo, translated as asking what cause there is. The Japanese example ends with the printed full stop even though the Portuguese translation has a question mark.
Nannǒ is glossed as 'without danger'. The caron on o distinguishes the printed form from the preceding unmarked Nanno and is not transferred between the entries.
Nanomena is redirected to the preferred form Nanamena and describes something bent or curved. The Latin Meliùs is the source's usage judgment; tor- begins torta on the next row.
Completes torta and gives arcada, 'arched', as the alternative description. The final body row and lower rule are both included in its crop.

Gives the adverb corresponding to the preceding bent or oblique adjective, preferring Nanameni to Nanomeni. The scan reads Meliùs, correcting the OCR transposition Melùis while retaining its grave accent.
Nanomenarazu is glossed as 'greatly'. The visibly separated Grande mente is retained, and Qi- begins the Japanese expression for high and low social ranks below.
Continues Qixẽ jǒgue and describes people of high and low rank becoming greatly agitated. The abbreviation in xẽ and the caron in jǒgue are preserved, as is the line-end division of nanomenarazu.
Completes nanomenarazu, supplies the Tai citation to book 30, and begins the translation 'high and low'. Tai remains upright, distinct from the italic bibliographic and Portuguese text.
Completes grãdemente and says that high and low alike became excited and disturbed. The printed nasal abbreviation and historical verb endings are preserved rather than recast in modern Portuguese.
Nanori is the verb for naming or announcing oneself, with its printed principal forms. Xinde- starts the concessive 'even if I die' example on the next row.

runs.text: mo nauo aguen tameni qemiǒ bacariuo

lines.note: Continues the resolve to raise one's name or reputation by announcing the ordinary name. The caron in qemiǒ and the attached object marker in bacariuo remain as printed; the verb follows below.

runs.text: Tos. Ainda que morra pera a-

lines.note: Completes the naming example and introduces the Tos citation and Portuguese translation. Enlargement shows the citation letters in italic type; the source's nanorǒzu mark is retained despite uneven ink.

runs.text: leuantar meu nome, ou cobrar fama nomear-

lines.note: Continues the wish to raise one's name or gain fame. Nomear- is supported by the visible e rather than OCR nomcar-, and the future construction is physically divided before me ei below.

runs.text: me ei ſòmente pello nome ordinario.

lines.note: Completes 'I shall name myself only by the ordinary name'. The separated me ei and the historical pello are preserved instead of modernizing the Portuguese future construction.

runs.text: Nome, com q̃ hũ ſe nomea ou aſina.

lines.note: The noun Nanori is the name by which one identifies or signs oneself. Enlargement reads aſina, with a single long s and an i, rather than OCR aſmna; no second s is supplied merely to match modern assina.
Nanoricaqe means announcing oneself while challenging another person. The following row identifies the opponent; the printed verb forms and historical prouocando are preserved.

runs.text: a outro que vai fugindo, ou eſta dißimulado.

lines.note: Specifies an opponent who is fleeing or remaining concealed. The printed dißimulado ligature is retained instead of expanded or respelled.
Begins an example with repeated self-announcement and a duration of about two time units. The printed repetition and the ba- division are both meaningful parts of the physical text.
Completes the account of fighting and supplies the Tai citation, book 21. The numeral is visibly 21 rather than OCR 2t; the Portuguese Nome- continues as Nomeandoſe below.

runs.text: andoſe por vezes, & prouocando pelejou co-

lines.note: Translates the repeated self-announcement and challenge followed by fighting. Co- begins como, introducing the approximate duration on the next row.
Completes 'for about two hours' as the source's translation of the duration. The close duashoras is retained rather than respaced, without imposing a modern conversion of the Japanese time unit.
Nanpǔ is a bad or dangerous wind. The example begins with the abbreviated Nã-; the following row completes the word and its particle rather than starting a different headword.
Completes Nãpǔni fanaſaruru, being driven or cast off by a dangerous wind. The scan shows pǔni, with u, its caron, and n, rather than OCR pôi; the gloss supports the wind-related construction.
Completes the phrase 'by the bad wind'. The short continuation closes the Nanpǔ example and is not confused with the following silver entry.
Nanriǒ is equated with Yoqi xirocane, good silver. The source's caron is retained here; the following row specifies the purity in the dictionary's own terms.

runs.text: de dez quilates que he a maisfina.

lines.note: Calls this ten-carat silver and the finest kind, recording the source's stated scale rather than correcting it to a modern assay convention. The printed maisfina join is preserved.
Nanrio is given as another name for the eighth month. Its headword has no visible long-vowel mark, unlike the preceding Nanriǒ, so the neighboring accent is not copied into it.
Completes 'the eighth moon, or month'. The nasal abbreviation in lũa is retained rather than expanded or modernized to lua.
Nanro denotes a difficult road, matching Catai michi. Tra- begins the Portuguese adjective trabalhoſo on the next row and is not part of the Japanese entry.
Completes trabalhoſo, describing the road as troublesome or arduous. It closes the unaccented Nanro entry before the separate Nanrô for a southern tower.
Nanrô is a southern tower or bastion, explained by Minamino yagura. The circumflex on o is visible and distinguishes the printed headword from the preceding road entry.

runs.text: torrinha que eſta da parte do Sul.

lines.note: Completes the definition as a small tower on the southern side. The diminutive torrinha and unaccented eſta remain as printed.
Nanſô denotes a south-facing window. Enlargement supports Minami rather than OCR Miuami; the Japanese explanation matches the Portuguese window gloss, whose direction continues below.
Completes pera parte do Sul, 'toward the southern side'. The source does not supply an article before parte here, and none is inserted.
Nantai means a male person and is then paired with nhotai, a female person. Ho- begins the Portuguese homem across the line break.
Completes the translation 'man and woman'. This physical continuation belongs to the paired example, not to a new entry or marginal note.
Nanten is described as a certain small yellow tree or shrub. The note records that descriptive gloss without supplying a botanical identification not printed on this page.
Nanto is an adverbial question 'how? or what?' The scan shows the alternative marker l and a second question mark, not OCR queẽ; yǔ- begins the concessive example below.
Completes Nanto yǔtemo, rendered 'however much you may say'. The physical split is inside yǔtemo and is retained instead of joining rows.

A different Nanto is the southern capital, explained by Minamino Miyaco. The Miyaco inside the Portuguese sentence is visibly spelled with i, correcting OCR Moyaco; the preceding Japanese explanation remains separate.

runs.text: do Sul, i, Nara, que he hũa cidade do reino

lines.note: Identifies that southern capital as Nara and describes it as a city in a named realm or province. Here Nara occurs within the continuing Portuguese explanation, not as an isolated synonym-only row.
Completes the location as Yamato. The whole phrase is visibly italic, including the initial Y that OCR had detached into roman type; Yamato is embedded in Portuguese.

runs.text: Golfão, ou paßagem perigoſa, ou dif-

lines.note: Another Nanto is a gulf or dangerous, difficult passage. The weak cross-stroke of the final letter supports f in dif-, rather than OCR long s; the word continues ficultoſa below and retains both printed f positions.
Completes difficultoſa, the adjective describing the hazardous passage. This is the final continuation of that Nanto sense, before the adverb Nantomo.
Nantomo is glossed as 'in no way' and introduces a negative example. The nasal abbreviation in nenhũa is retained without expanding it.
Gives an example of something that cannot be expressed. The source's iuarenu and attached cotogia are preserved, and the Portuguese relative clause continues below.

runs.text: por nenhũa via ſe pode dizer, ou explicar.

lines.note: Completes the explanation: something that cannot be said or explained by any means. The Portuguese negative construction corresponds to the Japanese iuarenu in the preceding row.
Nantomo catomo receives the same adverbial meaning as Nantomo. Idem points to the preceding 'in no way' explanation rather than adding an independent positive sense.
Nantonaritomo means 'in any manner'. The Portuguese ma- continues maneira below and is not a divided Japanese form.
Completes maneira and closes the 'in any manner' entry. This row is body text, unlike the separate signature and catchword that appear farther down.
Nantoxite asks 'how?', restated as 'in what manner'. The source's joined Deque and its i marker are retained; ma- continues into the final body word.

Completes maneira? and the Nantoxite definition. The unrelated Y y gathering signature and Nanto catchword occupy other positions on the same baseline and have been separated into furniture zones, not deleted or included in this gloss.
